scenes.tts: Hold your breath. Carbon dioxide accumulates, and oxygen falls. Yet what defeats you is mostly the carbon dioxide piling up, not oxygen running out. Why is the controller built that way?
scenes.visual: Breath held, airway closed: a carbon dioxide gauge rises, an oxygen gauge falls, a question mark over the controller between them.

scenes.tts: Two questions: where does the rhythm come from, and what sets how hard it drives the muscles? The rhythm comes from the medulla, from a small region called the pre Botzinger complex. Smith and colleagues found it in a neonatal rat brainstem in a dish. That is a reduced preparation, not the adult human circuit. At rest, the drive is largely chemical.
scenes.visual: Medulla block with the pre-Botzinger complex sending rhythm to the muscles; removing the block stops the output in the rat preparation; chemistry thickens the arrow.

scenes.tts: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood brain barrier and releases hydrogen ions in brain fluid. The brain mainly senses those ions, not the molecule itself. In mice, retrotrapezoid neurons are proton sensitive and project to the pre Botzinger complex. Which cells do the sensing is still open. The carotid body sits at the fork of each carotid artery. It is the main peripheral chemoreceptor for arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH.
scenes.visual: Left: CO2 crosses a barrier bar and becomes hydrogen ions that excite the retrotrapezoid chip, which projects to the pre-Botzinger chip; right: the carotid body at a fork, sending a nerve to the brainstem.

It is the main peripheral chemoreceptor for arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH.

scenes.tts: Against arterial P C O two, human ventilation rises along a roughly straight line. Against alveolar P O two, the curve is shallow above about sixty millimetres of mercury. It steepens as it enters roughly fifty to sixty. Weil and colleagues measured it under isocapnia. Added inspired carbon dioxide held alveolar P C O two at its resting value. Without that clamp, breathing harder lowers P C O two, which restrains ventilation.
scenes.visual: Two plots drawn in turn: a straight line against PCO2 and a shallow-then-steep curve against PO2 with a 50 to 60 band; a clamp note, then a chain showing breathing harder, PCO2 down, ventilation restrained.
scenes.caption: Against arterial PCO2, human ventilation rises along a roughly straight line. Against alveolar PO2, the curve is shallow above about 60 mmHg. It steepens as it enters roughly 50 to 60. Weil and colleagues measured it under isocapnia. Added inspired carbon dioxide held alveolar PCO2 at its resting value. Without that clamp, breathing harder lowers PCO2, which restrains ventilation.

scenes.tts: Take an adult at rest at sea level. Arterial P C O two is about forty millimetres of mercury. Arterial P O two is about one hundred. That is the steep part of the carbon dioxide line, and the flat part of the oxygen curve. A small P C O two error gives a large ventilation change. A small P O two error gives almost none. Oxygen's leverage lies elsewhere on its axis.
scenes.visual: Resting dots placed at 40 on the CO2 line and 100 on the O2 curve; a small step along each: ventilation jumps on the CO2 plot, hardly moves on the O2 plot.

scenes.tts: The breath hold ends at the apnea break point. The carbon dioxide signal usually arrives first, though no simple blood gas rule fully explains it. Eighteen volunteers with little freediving experience held repeated maximal breaths, face in cold water. Fifteen seconds of hyperventilation lowered starting end tidal P C O two. It fell from twenty nine to seventeen point four millimetres of mercury, in the thirteen with usable gas data. The mean hold grew from one hundred eleven to one hundred thirty three seconds. The mean saturation nadir fell from ninety three point six to ninety point six percent. Hyperventilation lowers the carbon dioxide signal and adds almost no oxygen. In an adult at rest, breathing is a carbon dioxide controller.
scenes.visual: Two cards, normal breathing and after 15 s of hyperventilation: starting PCO2 down, hold bar longer, saturation nadir lower; ends on the rule.
scenes.caption: The breath hold ends at the apnea break point. The carbon dioxide signal usually arrives first, though no simple blood gas rule fully explains it. 18 volunteers with little freediving experience held repeated maximal breaths, face in cold water. 15 seconds of hyperventilation lowered starting end-tidal PCO2. It fell from 29.0 to 17.4 mmHg, in the 13 with usable gas data. The mean hold grew from 111 to 133 seconds. The mean saturation nadir fell from 93.6 to 90.6 percent. Hyperventilation lowers the carbon dioxide signal and adds almost no oxygen. In an adult at rest, breathing is a carbon dioxide controller.
